C0600.d: The position loop that drives the range actuator to a target does not reach or hold it: commanded and measured position stay apart for too long, although sensor and drive circuit pass their own checks. Magna describes such a loop for a transfer case range shift, with speed profiles per shift phase and PID control over the last tenth of travel down to a stop at the target.
s: Range shift incomplete, indicator flashes
4WD service message and range shifts blocked
Noise from the transfer case while the motor hunts for position
c: Stiff range fork, cam or shift rail slows the actuator
Weak shift motor or low supply voltage
Learned end positions no longer match the hardware
Play between sensor target and shift mechanism

C0601.d: An active air dam is a panel below the front bumper that an electric drive lowers at speed to reduce drag and raises for slow driving, towing or rough ground. Ford's patent for this design moves the panel with two motor-driven screw jacks under command of the PCM or body module over LIN or CAN; a GM patent closes the loop with position, motor current and back-EMF feedback.
s: Active Air Dam System Fault message in the cluster
Air dam no longer moves and stays raised or lowered
Slightly higher fuel use on the highway when stuck raised
c: Actuator connector loose, unplugged or corroded after water entry
Wire broken in the exposed harness behind the bumper, often after impact or road debris
Open motor winding or internal fault in the air dam actuator

C0602.d: C0602 says the control line to the air dam actuator is held below its expected voltage, most often because a motor lead touches ground or because water has bridged pins in the connector. Smart H-bridge drivers such as the DRV8873-Q1 see a grounded output as overcurrent, trip within a few microseconds and turn that half-bridge off, so the motor never gets drive.
s: Air dam warning message in the instrument cluster
Air dam stays in one position
Fault returns as soon as the system commands movement
c: Actuator wire chafed through and touching the body or frame
Water and corrosion in the actuator connector after a damaged seal
Shorted motor or electronics inside the actuator

C0603.d: With C0603 the air dam control circuit reads above its permitted level, which points to a lead shorted to battery voltage or to another powered wire in the front-end harness. Motor driver ICs like the DRV8873-Q1 list a short to battery as a separate protected fault and disable the affected output.
s: Air dam system fault message
Air dam does not deploy at highway speed
Possible blown fuse for the air dam circuit
c: Control wire shorted to a battery-fed wire in the front harness
Fault in the actuator electronics holding the line high
Wrong pin assignment or splice after a previous bumper or harness repair

C0604.d: C0604 is the air dam code that makers really publish: the panel does not reach or hold its commanded position even though the circuit itself looks sound. Ford stores C0604:00 in the PCM of 2021–2023 F-150s, often with a cluster warning that the air dam system has failed; its fixes are new left and right actuators for an actuator firmware issue (SSM 51718), a PCM reflash (TSB 24-2404, later 25-2155 and 25-2236) and, o
s: Active Air Dam System Fault See Manual message
Air dam hangs down or does not retract
Clunk from the front end when driving at moderate speed or decelerating
Check engine lamp on some Ram trucks
c: Actuator firmware or PCM software level with known false or real faults (Ford F-150)
Broken bolts between actuator and air dam, panel hangs
Air dam bent, cracked or jammed after ground contact or debris
Water or corrosion in the actuator connector
Air dam lip rubbing on the front fascia

C0605.d: The steering wheel angle sensor tells the stability system how far and how quickly the driver turns. C0605 means its circuit is open or no usable signal arrives at all: a broken supply, ground or signal wire, an unplugged connector or a dead sensor.
s: ESC/stability control warning lamp on, system off
Traction control and lane or parking assistants may be unavailable
Steering angle reads zero or not available in scan data
c: Connector at the steering column loose or not latched after airbag or column work
Broken supply, ground or signal wire in the column harness

C0606.d: C0606 flags a steering angle signal or sensor supply that reads too low, as caused by a short to ground, a sagging supply or an output stuck at the bottom of its range. In the Kelsey-Hayes design the two phase lines swing between roughly 0.6 V and 4.4 V on a 5 V feed, and anything below the lower band is a fault; Bosch's PWM sensor maps −720° to +720° onto 10–90 % duty cycle, so a line pinned to ground leaves that wi
s: ESC warning lamp on and stability control unavailable
Steering angle in scan data pinned at one end value
Driver assistance messages about limited function
c: Signal wire chafed against the steering column and shorted to ground
Low sensor supply from a weak battery or a damaged feed circuit

C0607.d: C0607 is the mirror image of C0606: the steering angle signal sits above its allowed ceiling. Usual reasons are a signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or to battery voltage, an open ground at the sensor, after which the line drifts up, or an internal fault driving the output to its top end.
s: ESC and traction control warning lamps on
Steering angle shown at an implausible maximum value
Lane keeping or park assist switched off
c: Signal wire shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground, signal floats high

C0608.d: C0608 covers a steering angle signal that is electrically in range but cannot be trusted: it jumps, drifts, freezes or disagrees with what yaw rate, lateral acceleration and wheel speeds imply. The Kelsey-Hayes patent rejects a centre offset that moves by more than about 15° after a dropout, and Bosch builds plausibility checks of the individual measuring channels into its GMR sensor.
s: ESC lamp on, sometimes only after a few turns or straight driving
Unexpected ESC braking interventions
Steering angle not zero with the wheels pointing straight
c: Sensor not zeroed after wheel alignment, steering or column repair
Steering wheel fitted off centre or toe out of adjustment
Worn or faulty sensor giving jumping or frozen values
Brief signal dropouts from a loose connector

C0609.d: The park brake switch is the driver's apply and release button for an electric parking brake; on some cars it also reports lever or button state to other modules. C0609 covers an electrical fault in its circuit, such as an open contact, a short to ground or supply, or an unplugged connector.
s: Park brake or drive system warning in the cluster
Parking brake does not respond to the button
Gear selection refused in some electric models
c: Connector at the switch or in the dash not fully engaged
Poor ground or control unit software (Audi Q4 e-tron case)
Worn, contaminated or corroded switch contacts, e.g. after spilled drinks

C060A.d: C060A means the park brake switch reports a state that does not change when it should, or that contradicts itself: a jammed or welded contact, a button held down mechanically, or paired contacts that disagree. EPB buttons carry duplicated contacts for safety; a TRW patent notes that the controller flags an error when the paired signals do not arrive within about 30 ms, and that a blocked actuator can close just one o
s: Park brake warning lamp or message
Brake does not apply or release from the button
Code returns right after clearing while the button is untouched
c: Button jammed by dirt, sticky residue or a broken housing
One contact of the redundant pair welded or worn
Object in the console pressing the button

C060B.d: On motor-on-caliper parking brakes, a small DC motor drives a gear stage and a spindle that pushes the rear piston; ZF quotes up to 19 kN clamping force with its early swash plate gearbox and up to 25 kN with a two-stage planetary set for heavy vehicles. C060B means the control unit (ESC module or separate EPB module) finds the drive circuit of the left motor open: broken lead, unplugged caliper connector or burnt wi
s: Red park brake lamp flashing or Service Parking Brake message
Left rear brake does not apply when the switch is pulled
Auto-hold or hill-start assist unavailable
c: Corroded or loose connector or extension harness at the left caliper
Wire broken where the harness flexes with the suspension
Open winding in the left actuator motor

C060C.d: C060C indicates that a drive line of the left parking brake motor is pulled toward ground. Typical reasons are a motor lead chafed against the body or axle, water standing in the caliper connector, or a shorted motor.
s: Park brake warning lamp and service message
Left rear brake does not apply or release
Fuse for the park brake motor may blow
c: Motor lead chafed and shorted to the body or axle
Water and corrosion in the left caliper connector

C060D.d: Here one of the two left motor leads reads high: it is shorted to battery voltage, or touches another live wire, so the low side of the bridge cannot pull it down. A bridge driver such as the DRV8873-Q1 detects an output shorted to the battery and disables the stage to protect itself.
s: Park brake warning lamp on
Left rear brake does not respond to the switch
Electronic pad change mode cannot be entered
c: Motor lead shorted to a battery-fed wire
Moisture bridging pins in the caliper connector
Failed driver stage in the brake control module

C060E.d: C060E is set when the left actuator is driven but does not build or keep the clamping force it should, so the brake effectively stays off. Bosch's EPB patents derive clamping force from motor current: during apply it rises as pads meet the disc and then levels off at the target force.
s: Vehicle may creep on a slope with the parking brake applied
Park brake warning lamp or message
Motor noise without the usual clamping sound at the left rear
c: Worn gearbox, belt or spindle inside the left actuator
Pads or piston not set up correctly after brake service without maintenance mode
High resistance in the left motor circuit limits motor torque

C060F.d: C060F is the reverse of C060E: the left actuator does not release, or the module cannot confirm that it has. An Advics patent recognises release by watching motor current while the motor runs backwards: once the current stops changing after a minimum time of around 200 ms, the clamping force is taken as zero and the motor runs on briefly to set pad clearance.
s: Left rear brake drags, smells hot or the car pulls away sluggishly
Park brake lamp stays on after release
Release message or refusal to drive off
c: Seized caliper piston or corroded spindle nut
Pads frozen or rusted to the disc after standing
Broken gear stage in the actuator

C0610.d: C0610 reports that the drive circuit of the right rear parking brake motor is open, so the controller switches its bridge but no motor current flows. Mitsubishi's 2023 Outlander PHEV shows how such a check works under its own code C10B0-01: during apply or release the ABS unit looks for an open motor circuit on the right side and reacts within about one second, then suspends the electric parking brake and hill start
s: Parking brake warning lamp and service message
Right rear caliper neither applies nor releases electrically
Hill start assist or auto hold unavailable
c: Right caliper motor connector unplugged, corroded or with pushed-back pins
Broken wire in the harness that flexes with the right rear suspension
Open winding or worn brushes in the right actuator motor
Blown fuse or fusible link feeding the parking brake output stage

C0611.d: C0611 means one of the two leads to the right parking brake motor is dragged toward ground. The harness to the right rear caliper rides on the suspension and passes close to the brake disc, so chafing against the knuckle or water in the plug are the usual suspects, followed by a shorted motor.
s: Parking brake warning lamp on
Right side does not apply; vehicle may roll on a slope if not in Park or in gear
Fuse for the parking brake circuit may blow
c: Motor lead chafed through at the right rear knuckle or bracket
Water and corrosion bridging pins in the right caliper connector
Internal short in the right actuator motor

C0612.d: With C0612 a lead of the right parking brake motor stays at or near battery voltage while the bridge tries to pull it low. Likely causes are a short to a live wire in the rear harness, a wrong splice after body or axle repair, or a defect in the output stage.
s: Service parking brake message and warning lamp
Right parking brake does not respond to the switch
Code may return as soon as an apply is commanded
c: Motor lead shorted to a battery-fed wire in the rear harness
Failed low-side switch in the control unit holding the lead high
Wrong pin or splice after an earlier harness or body repair

C0613.d: C0613 covers a right actuator that is powered but fails to clamp. The wiring is intact, yet the module never sees the motor turn or the current rise that marks pads pressed against the disc.
s: Parking brake warning lamp and message
Parked vehicle may creep on a slope
No motor noise from the right rear when the brake is applied
c: Stripped gear, slipping belt or broken spindle inside the right actuator
Motor seized by corrosion after water entry
High resistance in the right circuit starving the motor of current
Pads or disc worn far beyond limit, or caliper not calibrated after a brake job

C0614.d: C0614 is set when the right parking brake will not let go, or when the module cannot confirm that it has. To release, the motor runs in reverse; Advics treats the force as released when, after a minimum run of roughly 200 ms, the current has settled, and then lets the motor run on briefly to restore pad clearance.
s: Right rear brake drags; car pulls or feels held back when driving off
Hot right rear wheel and burning smell
Parking brake warning and release request not completed
c: Seized caliper piston or corroded spindle nut on the right side
Pads rusted to the disc after the car stood for a long time
Jammed gearbox or damaged motor in the right actuator

C0615.d: C0615 points at the circuit that feeds or enables the parking brake control electronics, not at a single caliper: it reads as open. Today the parking brake logic often runs as a software block inside the ESC unit (VDA recommendation 305-100), while the host supplies the motor power stage; a few cars keep a separate module.
s: Electric parking brake inoperative on both sides
Parking brake warning lamp and service message
Auto hold and hill start assist unavailable
c: Blown fuse or fusible link in the parking brake power feed
Loose or corroded terminal on the power or enable line at the module
Broken wire between fuse box and module
Internal fault in the module's supply stage

C0616.d: C0616 is the one code in this range that GM really uses. Its 2025 EBCM tables file over twenty parking brake self-tests under it, all Type C without MIL: the left and right H-bridge supplies may not differ by more than 12 % at 8–20 V, the current measuring path must read 10.5–17 A in its self-test, the motor voltage must stay between 7 and 18 V for 700 ms, plus watchdog, ASIC and rollaway checks.
s: Service Parking Brake message in the driver information center
Parking brake warning lamp; parking brake may be inhibited
Check engine lamp on some GM models
c: Software anomaly in the brake module (GM 2024 HD trucks, fixed by reprogramming)
Weak battery, poor ground or charging fault pushing motor voltage outside its window
Internal hardware fault in the parking brake ASIC, bridge or measuring path
Parking brake assembly check not completed after module replacement

C0617.d: C0617 says the supply or control line feeding the parking brake electronics reads too low. Because both caliper motors draw several amps when they clamp, a weak battery, a poor ground or a corroded feed shows up here first.
s: Parking brake warning lamp, often together with other low-voltage messages
Parking brake applies slowly or not at all
Hill start assist unavailable
c: High resistance in the module ground or power feed
Control or enable line shorted to ground

C0618.d: C0618 is the overvoltage counterpart of C0617: the feed or control line of the parking brake electronics reads above its window. A regulator fault in the alternator or DC/DC converter, jump starting with a booster set to 24 V, or a short between the enable line and a live wire are the usual reasons.
s: Parking brake warning lamp, possibly with a battery or charging warning
Parking brake does not respond to the switch
Other modules may log overvoltage codes at the same time
c: Faulty voltage regulator in the alternator or DC/DC converter
Overvoltage from a jump starter or charger on a 24 V setting
Enable or control line shorted to a battery-fed wire

C0619.d: Pedal position sensors are taught their rest value, and C0619 says the offset found for channel A lies outside the band the controller will accept. A Hitachi patent on electric boosters learns the stroke sensor zero only with the pedal released and no brake request, and treats a zero beyond a prescribed range as a sensor fault.
s: Brake or brake system warning lamp; check engine lamp on some vehicles
Brake lights, cruise control or shifting behave as if the pedal were pressed
Reduced brake assist or regenerative braking on electrified models
c: Intermittent connection in the sensor circuit that skewed the learned value
Pedal not returning fully (floor mat, stiff pivot, wrong adjustment)
Sensor drifted or fitted out of position after replacement
Learn procedure skipped or disturbed after sensor or module service

C061A.d: C061A is the same learn-limit check for the second channel, B. Many pedal sensors hold two independent elements; on GM trucks since 2012 one potentiometer feeds the ECM and the other the BCM, each with its own 5 V reference, ground and signal.
s: Brake system warning or message
Mismatch between modules about pedal state, e.g. brake lights versus cruise control
Shift interlock or start function may act up
c: Dropout or fretting corrosion on the channel B reference, ground or signal pin
Learn done in only one module, or the pedal moved during the learn
Pedal rest position changed by a mat, bracket damage or adjustment
Drifting second element inside the pedal sensor

C061B.d: C061B is not a brake fault at all. It records that the engine control module told the brake module to switch traction control off, usually because the engine can no longer cut torque on demand.
s: Traction control off lamp or Service Traction Control message
Stability control may also be unavailable
Engine codes stored, sometimes with the check engine lamp
c: Engine misfire or other engine fault that blocks torque reduction
Electronic throttle or torque model fault stored in the ECM
Corrupt or missing torque messages between engine and brake module
ECM software issue setting the disable request without a real fault

C061C.d: Variable effort steering changes how hard a hydraulic system steers with road speed. In GM's Magnasteer a coil and permanent magnets on the rotary valve add or subtract from the torsion bar's stiffness; the GM and Steering Solutions patent EP2028081B1 describes this actuator, and ±3 A coil current is cited in a later patent.
s: Steering effort no longer changes with speed
Heavier steering when parking or lighter, nervous steering on the highway
Steering or stability warning on some vehicles
c: Connector at the steering gear loose, corroded or soaked with fluid
Open actuator coil inside the steering gear
Broken wire between control module and steering gear

C061D.d: C061D flags an actuator line held too low, most often a coil lead shorted to the steering gear housing or to the vehicle body. The Magnasteer coil sits in the cast valve housing, which forms part of its magnetic circuit, so insulation damage there grounds the winding; checking each coil terminal against the housing is a standard test.
s: Speed-dependent steering feel lost
Steering feels the same at all speeds
Fuse for the steering actuator may blow
c: Actuator coil insulation broken down to the steering gear housing
Actuator wire chafed against subframe or exhaust heat shield
Failed output stage in the controlling module

C061E.d: C061E means an actuator line reads above what the controller expects, typically a lead shorted to battery voltage or a driver stage stuck on. Delphi describes Magnasteer as electronically modulating the magnetic torsional rate, with coil polarity deciding whether effort rises or falls; a line stuck high can therefore hold the actuator in one direction or stop the bridge from regulating.
s: Unusually heavy or unusually light steering that does not change with speed
Steering warning message on some vehicles
c: Actuator lead shorted to a battery-fed wire
Output transistor in the module stuck on
Wrong pinning after a steering gear swap

C061F.d: C061F covers an actuator circuit that is electrically intact but does not behave as commanded: the current does not follow the request, or the expected change in effort fails to show up. In Magnasteer the coil runs from about −3 A to +3 A, and the current reverses around mid speed, so tracking errors appear as wrong feel in town or on the highway.
s: Steering effort wrong for the speed or changing unexpectedly
Pull to one side with no alignment fault
Steering warning on some vehicles
c: Magnetic null shifted from valve centre, damaged magnet ring
Sticking rotary valve from contaminated fluid
High resistance in connector or wiring limiting coil current
Wrong or missing vehicle speed input to the controlling module

C0620.d: Some steering systems that vary effort or ratio carry a second actuator whose only job is safety: a solenoid lock that blocks the motor or gear so the wheel turns the wheels directly. Delphi's patent combining Magnasteer with an active steering actuator uses a solenoid that is energised to unlock and drops into lock without power; JTEKT and Continental lock their superimposed steering the same fail-safe way.
s: Variable steering function disabled; steering works with a fixed characteristic
Steering system warning
Possible click or no click from the steering when switching on
c: Connector to the lock solenoid unplugged or corroded
Open lock solenoid coil, for example after overheating
Broken wire between the steering module and the lock

C0621.d: C0621 reports the lock or safety actuator line held too low. In JTEKT's variable-ratio design a PNP transistor switches the lock coil, and the ECU holds the line low on purpose when it wants to lock, for instance after a motor or sensor fault or a broken cable.
s: Variable ratio or effort function off
Steering warning lamp or message
c: Lock solenoid wire shorted to ground in the column or gear harness
Shorted turns in the lock solenoid
Failed drive transistor in the steering module

C0622.d: C0622 is the critical direction for a fail-safe lock: the actuator line reads high even when the controller wants it off. Since the lock in these designs releases when powered, a line shorted to battery voltage would keep it open when it should engage, so the safety path no longer works.
s: Steering system warning; variable function switched off
No noticeable change in normal steering
c: Lock solenoid wire shorted to a battery-fed circuit
Drive transistor in the module stuck on

C0623.d: C0623 covers a lock or safety actuator whose circuit is sound but whose action does not match the command: it does not release when energised, does not engage in time, or its current is implausible. JTEKT's lock coil first gets full duty for about one second to pull the arm free, then 60 % below 13 V or 40 % above 14 V to hold it, which keeps the coil at or below 100 °C instead of near 200 °C.
s: Steering warning and variable function off
Clicking or knocking from the steering column at start or stop
Steering wheel slightly off-centre after the system locks
c: Sticking lock arm or pin, worn lock teeth
Solenoid weakened by heat, pull-in force too low
Weak or broken return spring, lock engages late

C0624.d: Variable effort steering tunes hydraulic assist to the situation, and besides road speed some systems also read a steering wheel sensor. Ford's variable-assist steering, first used on the 1988 Lincoln Continental, fed its module from an optical sensor tracking how the wheel turns; a Ford patent describes that encoder with 20 slots and two detectors, good for 4.5° steps, and drops the actuator current during quick eva
s: Steering effort no longer reacts to quick wheel movements
Effort stays at one level or follows only road speed
Steering warning on some vehicles
c: Loose or corroded connector at the steering column sensor
Wire broken where the harness flexes in the steering column
Failed sensor, for example a dead optical detector

C0625.d: Here the sensor signal is electrically present but its content does not add up. With an incremental steering wheel sensor the module derives rate or angle from pulse counts; a Ford patent computes steering rate from the counts in a fixed sampling window, so lost pulses give a wrong rate.
s: Steering effort changes unexpectedly while turning
Variable assist switched off with a fixed steering feel
Steering or stability warning on some vehicles
c: Dirt or damage on the encoder disc causing lost pulses
Intermittent contact at the connector producing short dropouts
Sensor loose or misaligned after column or steering work
Implausible road speed input used for the cross-check

C0626.d: C0626 means the signal of the variable effort steering sensor reads below the lowest level the module accepts. A Kelsey-Hayes patent shows the typical window for such a steering wheel sensor: with a 5 V supply each channel switches between roughly 0.6 V and 4.4 V, and anything under the lower band counts as low.
s: Variable assist disabled, steering effort fixed
Steering warning lamp or message
c: Signal wire chafed through and shorted to ground
5 V sensor feed missing or pulled down by another fault
Sensor output stage failed and stuck low

C0627.d: The high counterpart: the sensor signal sits above the top of the band the module treats as valid. In the Kelsey-Hayes design a healthy channel peaks near 4.4 V on a 5 V supply, so a reading close to the supply rail or beyond it points to a short to the reference or to battery voltage, or to a broken sensor ground that lets the input float high.
s: Variable assist disabled, steering effort fixed
Steering warning lamp or message
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or to battery voltage
Open sensor ground letting the signal float high
Sensor output stage failed and stuck high

C0628.d: C0628 says the unit that runs variable effort steering fails its own function checks. On GM's Magnasteer that unit was a separate module in 1996–97 and became part of the brake control module from 1998.
s: Steering effort no longer changes with speed
Heavy steering when parking or light steering at highway speed
Steering, ABS or stability warning where the brake module hosts the function
c: Internal fault in the controlling module or its coil driver stage
Low or unstable supply voltage so the commanded current cannot be reached
Corrupt calibration or software after a module replacement or flash

C0629.d: C0629 flags a mismatch between what the variable effort steering module expects and what is fitted. Variable-effort gears exist in versions that cannot be swapped blindly: replacement racks come with or without the EVO solenoid, and GM's second Magnasteer generation dropped the permanent magnet and only raises effort with speed, whereas the first one reverses coil current around 45 mph.
s: Variable assist inactive after a steering or module repair
Steering effort behaves the wrong way round, heavy when slow
Steering warning on some vehicles
c: Replacement steering gear of the wrong variant, for example without actuator
Module from another vehicle or not configured for this equipment
Actuator connected with reversed polarity after a repair

C062A.d: The variable effort steering module, or its coil driver, reports a temperature above its permitted limit. Heat matters twice here: a GM patent on magnetic variable effort steering notes that fluid viscosity, magnet properties and coil current all drift with temperature and either fits a sensor in the fluid sump or infers temperature from the current error.
s: Variable effort reduced or switched off temporarily
Steering feel changes after hard use and returns after cooling
c: Very high underhood or fluid temperature, for example after long parking manoeuvres in heat
Partly shorted coil drawing excess current and heating the driver
Faulty internal temperature measurement reporting heat that is not there

C062B.d: C062B is set when the module or its coil driver reads a temperature below the range it is designed for. Automotive driver chips such as TI's DRV8873-Q1 are specified down to an ambient of −40 °C, so a lower reading means either an extreme cold soak or a measurement that has failed.
s: Variable effort inactive after a cold start
Heavy or uneven steering until the system warms up
c: Vehicle parked for a long time in severe frost
Open or failed temperature measurement inside the module or at the fluid sensor
Moisture or corrosion at the connector distorting the reading

C062C.d: C062C judges whether the second drive, B, of an electric brake booster moves as commanded; the circuit may be intact. Boosters like Bosch's iBooster turn motor torque through a three-stage gear into force on the master cylinder, and in redundant layouts such as a Hyundai Mobis design a dual-winding motor is fed by two power modules, each able to carry the whole current command alone if the other is declared failed.
s: Brake system or brake assist warning
Harder pedal or reduced assist in some situations
Driver assistance functions with automatic braking restricted
c: Worn or damaged motor B, for example bearing or winding damage
Fault in the power module or driver stage feeding side B
Binding in gear stage or booster mechanism
Booster control software needing an update

C062D.d: C062D means the ABS valve group does not work as expected, although no single valve or plain supply fault explains it. Mitsubishi is the one maker that maps it publicly: in the 2023 Outlander PHEV brake unit, valve relay code C1048-92 shows as C062D, set within 2 s with normal supply and the system switched on, with ASC, ABS, brake lamp and MIL after one trip; bulletin 23-35-002 adds C1048-01 to the same number.
s: ABS, stability control and brake warning lamps on
Check engine lamp on (Mitsubishi)
ABS, traction control and electric parking brake unavailable
c: Internal fault in the ABS control unit or its valve relay
Weak supply through fuse, fusible link, wiring or 12 V battery
Corroded or loose connector at the hydraulic unit

C062E.d: The active air dam actuators run from the vehicle battery while the PCM or body module commands them over LIN or CAN, as Ford's patent lays out. C062E reports that the supply reaching the actuator or its module is too low to move the panel safely.
s: Air dam no longer moves and stays in its last position
Air dam fault message in the cluster
Low-voltage codes in other modules at the same time
c: Loose or corroded ground point in the front harness
Water or washer fluid wicking into an inline connector
Weak battery or low charging voltage
High resistance in fuse or feed wire to the actuator

C062F.d: C062F is the overvoltage side: the supply at the air dam actuator or its module lies above the permitted window. Ford's patent powers the screw-jack actuators from the vehicle battery, so a regulator fault in the charging system, jump-starting with a higher voltage or a load dump spike can push the feed too high.
s: Air dam stops moving, often together with other overvoltage codes
Air dam fault message in the cluster
Flickering lights or charging warning if the regulator is at fault
c: Charging system overvoltage from a faulty regulator
Jump start or battery charger with excessive voltage
Faulty voltage measurement inside the actuator electronics

C0630.d: C0630 says the air dam panel itself does not move although the actuator is driven and reports sensible values. GM's patent defines exactly this case: if measured position and motor current agree with each other but both differ from the commanded position, or back-EMF shows unusual load, the panel is at fault rather than sensor or drive.
s: Air dam hangs down or does not deploy
Air dam fault message in the cluster
Scraping on ramps or slightly higher fuel use on the highway
c: Panel bent or jammed after ground contact, debris or a kerb
Broken bolts between actuator and panel
Ice, snow or packed mud blocking the guides
Worn or seized screw jack in the actuator

C0631.d: A front axle disconnect separates the front shaft from the driveline when only the rear or primary wheels need to drive, cutting drag; a BorgWarner patent shows a shift fork sliding a splined sleeve, with a cone synchroniser matching speeds first. Ford uses C0631 in the AWD module of 2020–2021 Explorer and Aviator built up to 30 Aug 2021: the powertrain malfunction (wrench) lamp comes on, often with C00A6, and the ca
s: Wrench or 4WD/AWD warning lamp on
All-wheel drive not available or front axle does not engage
Possible noise from the front axle area
c: Failed disconnect actuator or intermediate shaft (Ford Explorer/Aviator 2020–2021)
Loose, corroded or damaged actuator connector
Shift sleeve or synchroniser binding, often from wear or fluid problems

C0632.d: C0632 concerns the electrical path that drives the front axle disconnect, not the shift itself. The actuator may be electromagnetic or electromechanical; BorgWarner's patent even reads its position from the coil's inductance, which changes between engaged and released.
s: 4WD/AWD service message or warning lamp
Front axle does not engage or disengage
c: Chafed or cut wires close to the actuator connector
Water or corrosion in the actuator or inline connector
Spread or pushed-out terminals in the connector

C0633.d: On all-wheel-drive systems that can uncouple the front axle, a speed sensor on a front shaft tells the controller how fast the uncoupled part turns, so it can match speeds before re-engaging. A BorgWarner patent uses a Hall sensor on the shift sleeve to read both speed and position and engages once the gap to wheel speed is within about ±100–200 rpm; an American Axle patent uses a pinion speed sensor the same way bef
s: AWD or 4WD warning messages in the cluster
All-wheel drive limited or not engaging
Possible oil seepage near the sensor
c: Sensor contaminated with axle oil (Ford Explorer/Aviator 2020)
Failed sensor or damaged wiring and connector
Wrong air gap or damaged sensor target on the shaft

C0634.d: Two brake pressure sensors that see the same hydraulic pressure should report nearly the same value; C0634 means sensors A and B disagree beyond the allowed margin, even if each signal is valid on its own. Which sensor bears which letter depends on the maker.
s: ABS, stability or brake system warning lamp on
Brake assist or driver assistance functions with automatic braking off
c: One sensor drifting in offset or gain
Fault in the brake control unit with integrated sensors, often replaced as a unit
Air or a blocked passage making the sensors see different pressures
Brake module software or calibration needing an update

C0635.d: C0635 flags a broken circuit at brake pressure sensor G: a supply, signal or ground wire without continuity, or a plug that has lost contact. No manufacturer publishes C0635 in this meaning, so it is unknown which part carries the letter G.
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Stability control and pressure-based brake functions switched off
c: Plug at the sensor or hydraulic unit loose, corroded or with pushed-back terminals
Broken supply, signal or ground wire in the sensor harness

C0636.d: The voltage of sensor G sits above anything a valid pressure can produce. A Toyota patent shows how a brake gets seven pressure sensors: one for the accumulator, two for the master cylinder chambers and four for the wheel cylinders, all read by the brake ECU.
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Live data shows high pressure with the pedal released
Brake assist and stability functions unavailable
c: Signal wire shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Open or high-resistance sensor ground lifting the output
Sensor G failed internally and driving its output to the top

C0637.d: C0637 reports that sensor G delivers less voltage than its lowest valid reading. Brake pressure sensors keep a live zero at rest, so a signal near 0 V means a fault rather than zero pressure: Saab's 9-5 ESP flags a pressure signal under 0.25 V lasting 0.1 s, and GM's 2016 hybrid brake module treats under 0.3 V for 0.1 s on its left rear wheel pressure sensor (sensor D there) as a short to ground, Type A.
s: ABS and ESC warning lamps on
Live data shows no pressure even when the pedal is pressed
c: Signal wire chafed and shorted to ground
5 V sensor reference shorted to ground or interrupted
Sensor G defective, often only replaceable with the hydraulic unit

C0638.d: Here sensor G produces a voltage inside its window, but the pressure it reports disagrees with what the system expects. Lucas/ZF describe the classic test for multi-sensor EHB units: after the driver brakes to a stop, the isolation valve stays closed and all wheel valves open, so three or more sensors share one pressure; the odd one out is the faulty sensor, with size and direction of its error.
s: ABS lamp and ESC telltale on
Stability control reduced or off, regenerative braking possibly limited
c: Zero point or gain of sensor G drifted
Pressure trapped in the circuit during the comparison or zero learn
Valve sticking so the sensor does not see the shared test pressure

C0639.d: Brake pressure sensor H has lost its electrical connection: an interrupted 5 V feed, signal or ground line, or a loose plug at the hydraulic unit. No published service data ties C0639 to a real part.
s: ABS and ESC lamps on, possibly flickering with vibration
ABS or stability control disabled
c: Sensor plug loose or terminals corroded
Supply, signal or ground conductor broken
Open measuring bridge or failed electronics inside the sensor

C063A.d: The output of pressure sensor H is too high to be real. C063A is not documented by any carmaker.
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, ESC unavailable
Implausibly high brake pressure in live data at rest
c: Signal line touching a 5 V or battery feed
Sensor ground open or high resistance
Sensor reports an internal fault or overpressure at its upper rail

C063B.d: C063B says sensor H reads below its valid floor. Unlike C063C the problem is electrical, not a believable but wrong pressure.
s: ABS and ESC lamps on
Brake assist and stability control not available
c: 5 V reference collapsed by a short in another sensor on the same feed
Sensor H without output due to an internal defect

C063C.d: Sensor H gives an electrically valid yet implausible pressure. In Toyota's eight-sensor patent the check connects a pressure source to a brake cylinder: both readings should then nearly match, and a gap beyond a threshold means one of the two sensors, the passage or the cylinder is at fault; the switch-over is preferably made at standstill.
s: ESC malfunction telltale and ABS lamp on
Changed pedal feel or reduced brake assistance
c: Offset or gain of sensor H drifted out of tolerance
Restricted passage or faulty brake cylinder so pressures really differ
Air in the brake fluid distorting the pressure build-up

C063D.d: A wire or contact of brake pressure sensor J is interrupted. No manufacturer ties C063D to a specific sensor.
s: Brake system or ESC warning lamp on
Pressure-controlled brake functions switched off
c: Spread or corroded terminal in the sensor connector
Conductor interrupted between sensor and control unit

C063E.d: C063E: sensor J sends more voltage than its range allows. GM's 2016 hybrid brake controller shows the method on a wheel pressure sensor: if the signal line exceeds 3.3 V and so no longer differs from the supply, a short to supply is stored after 0.1 s with the ignition on, rated Type A.
s: Brake or ESC warning lamp on
Live data shows brake pressure although no one is braking
c: Signal line shorted to the sensor supply
Sensor ground interrupted, output lifted through the input divider
Sensor J electronics failed with output stuck high

C063F.d: The signal of brake pressure sensor J is stuck below its lower limit. Ipgate's double-stroke-piston patent fits one pressure sensor to each brake circuit and checks the delivered fluid volume against the pressure-volume curve of that circuit; such a circuit sensor is one possible J position, though no manufacturer confirms the letter.
s: ABS, traction and stability warning lamps on
ABS and ESC inoperative until the next ignition cycle
c: Broken feed or signal wire pulled to 0 V by the module input
Failed sensing element in sensor J

C0640.d: C0640 marks sensor J as valid in voltage but wrong in content. In plunger-based brakes the pressure can be cross-checked against what the actuator did: Ipgate compares delivered piston volume with the pressure-volume curve and closes the inlet valves one by one to find a leaking circuit, while Continental's one-box layout carries separate sensors for master cylinder and pressure supply that can be set against each ot
s: Brake warning and ESC lamps on
Longer pedal travel or reduced brake boost in fallback mode
c: Sensor J drifting so its zero correction exceeds the limit
Leak or air in the brake circuit so pressure and delivered volume disagree

C0641.d: Brake pressure sensor K has an open circuit. Because the letter I is skipped in this series, K stands for a tenth pressure sensor, which is rare in cars; no carmaker publishes C0641 and the assignment is unknown.
s: ESC or ABS warning lamp on
Stability control off, basic ABS may remain available
c: Poor contact between sensor and module or harness connector
Open conductor where an external harness is used

C0642.d: C0642 means the output of sensor K exceeds its upper limit. Electro-hydraulic brakes like Mercedes' Sensotronic Brake Control work with a high-pressure accumulator and a pedal value sensor with two Hall elements; during a pre-drive check the unit pressurises the calipers to test, among other things, its pressure sensors.
s: Brake system and ESC warning lamps on
Brake lights or hold functions may be requested wrongly on some systems
c: Signal shorted to 5 V or battery voltage
Internal fault of sensor K signalled at the upper rail

C0643.d: Sensor K reports less voltage than any valid pressure would give. Bendix's truck ESP treats brake demand and load sensors individually and, if one of them fails, disables only ESP while ABS and traction control carry on; this graded reaction shows why the code may leave basic ABS working.
s: ESC lamp on, ESC switched off
ABS and traction control may keep working
c: Broken sensor supply read as 0 V through the input pull-down

C0644.d: The voltage from sensor K is in range, yet the pressure is not believable. Bendix's EC-80 stores a plausibility error when the primary and secondary brake demand sensors disagree and asks for a static calibration after an ECU swap.
s: ABS and ESC lamps on until a later successful check
Stability control reduced, pedal may feel different in fallback mode
c: Sensor K offset or gain drifted
Sensor values not re-learned after module replacement
Leak, air or a valve that does not seal distorting the pressure

C0645.d: C0645 reports lost continuity in the circuit of brake pressure sensor L, the eleventh letter of the series because I is not used. That is far beyond a normal car: a Bosch patent names one, three or five sensors as the usual ESP layouts and calls five the current maximum.
s: ESC and ABS warning lamps on
Pressure-based functions such as brake assist or hill hold unavailable
c: Spring contact between sensor and module board bent, dirty or corroded
Plug or harness of an externally mounted sensor without continuity

C0646.d: C0646 means the signal of brake pressure sensor L lies above the band a real pressure can produce. A Kelsey-Hayes patent spells out the logic for a bridge-type brake sensor: a healthy output stays between zero and the supply voltage, so a reading equal to supply points to an open circuit, not to maximum pressure.
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Stability control or electronic brake pressure control switched off
c: Sensor ground open, so the signal floats up to supply level
Signal line shorted to the 5 V reference or battery voltage
Sensor electronics driving the output to its upper limit

C0647.d: Sensor L reads below its lowest valid value. In the Kelsey-Hayes scheme a near-zero bridge output is read as a probable short, because the sensor never reaches 0 V with a working circuit.
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Brake assist and stability control unavailable
c: Sensor supply missing or pulled down
Amplifier or input stage in the brake control module defective

C0648.d: Sensor L delivers an electrically valid signal whose pressure does not fit the situation. Commercial vehicle EBS shows how such a check works with many sensors: WABCO's tractor EBS has pressure sensors in the front axle relay valve, in each channel of the rear axle modulator and in the trailer control valve.
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, sometimes only after several brake applications
Uneven or reduced electronic brake force distribution
c: Sticking valve, leak or trapped pressure in the measured circuit
Calibration data not matching the fitted sensor after a repair

C0649.d: The circuit of brake pressure sensor M, the twelfth in the series, has no continuity. Where so many pressure inputs exist, they are often not reachable from outside: WABCO notes that the two rear axle pressure sensors of its truck EBS are wired inside the axle modulator, so the cabling cannot be tested from outside and a fault means work on the modulator.
s: Brake or ABS warning lamp on
Electronic pressure control replaced by a fallback mode
c: Loose or corroded plug at an external sensor or at the modulator
Open in the internal wiring of the modulator or hydraulic unit
Broken wire in the sensor harness

C064A.d: C064A: the voltage from sensor M exceeds what any valid pressure would give. On WABCO's Trailer EBS D the brake pressure sensor of an extra EBS relay valve, for example on a drawbar trailer's front axle, draws its supply from the trailer modulator and returns its actual value as an analog signal; all active sensors share supply outputs that are protected against short circuits.
s: Brake or ABS warning lamp on
Load-dependent or electronic pressure control disabled
c: Signal pin shorted to the sensor supply or battery voltage
Open sensor ground or signal line letting the input float high
Sensor output stuck at its upper limit

C064B.d: Sensor M sits below its lower signal limit. Because modules often supply several pressure sensors together, a single low code can be the visible part of a wider fault: WABCO's trailer modulator powers all active sensors jointly, so a short on one sensor supply can pull others down too, and codes for neighbouring letters may then appear at the same time.
s: Warning lamp on, possibly with further pressure sensor codes
Electronic brake functions reduced to a fallback mode
c: Shared sensor supply shorted, pulling several sensors low
Signal line or contact of sensor M shorted to ground

C064C.d: Sensor M stays inside its electrical window, but the pressure it reports is not believable. Trailer EBS shows an active test: when the control pressure exceeds 0.3 bar, WABCO's modulator switches its redundancy valve to reservoir pressure and starts EBS braking; during the stop it briefly switches back and uses its internal actual-pressure sensors to confirm that pneumatic pressure is present, otherwise it changes to
s: Warning lamp on after a brake application
Braking switched to a backup mode with less precise pressure control
c: Sensor reading drifted from the true pressure
Valve in the measured circuit not switching as commanded
Contamination or air at the sensor port

C064D.d: C064D concerns an interrupted circuit at brake pressure sensor N, the thirteenth of the series. Larger sensor counts push makers towards digital links.
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on, often with other pressure sensor codes
Stability control and brake assist unavailable
c: Open in a line or plug shared by several sensors
Poor contact at the sensor plug or spring contact

C064E.d: The signal of sensor N is above its permitted maximum. What the brake does next is described well for truck EBS: WABCO checks every analog pressure sensor signal against its authorised values; if one is lost, the module may keep producing electrical brake pressure by auxiliary means with limited accuracy, and if electronic control is impossible the axle falls back on purely pneumatic backup braking.
s: Brake or ESC warning lamp on
Less precise brake pressure control or pure backup braking
c: Signal shorted to sensor supply or battery voltage
Sensor electronics reporting full scale or an internal fault

C064F.d: C064F: sensor N reports less than its smallest valid signal. In integrated units the sensor element and its evaluation are split: Continental Teves fits a bare measuring bridge into the hydraulic block and leaves amplification and offset to an IC in the module, while Actronics, which repairs such units, names the ATE MK60 with its internal pressure sensor as the system with the most pressure sensor problems and recom
s: ABS/ESC warning lamp on
Stability control unavailable
c: Internal pressure sensor of the hydraulic unit failed
Signal contact or line shorted to ground
Evaluation IC in the control module defective

C0650.d: Sensor N reports a pressure that is electrically valid but disagrees with the commanded or expected value. WABCO's truck EBS runs a matching test: with a defined magnetic flux in the proportional valve a minimum brake pressure must build up at the front axle brakes, or at the valve that controls the trailer, and when the vehicle brakes via pneumatic backup the rear axle must reach a set minimum once the front exceeds
s: Warning lamp on after braking
Pressure control falls back to an emergency mode
c: Valve or modulator not building the commanded pressure
Leak or air in the measured circuit

C0651.d: C0651 reports an open circuit at the second speed sensor of the left front wheel. Sensor B exists only where a wheel carries two independent speed signals, mainly in redundant brake systems for automated driving.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Automated driving or redundant brake functions unavailable
c: Broken wire in the sensor B cable near the wheel
Plug of the second channel loose or corroded
Second sensing element inside the sensor failed open

C0652.d: The second left front wheel speed signal is present but implausible. With two channels per wheel the module has a direct partner to compare: Volvo Truck's patent for a dual-element sensor merges both signals with an integrity index, averages them while they agree within a band, takes the higher value when both run but differ, and drops a channel that reads zero.
s: Driver assistance or redundant braking warning
Automated functions withdrawn while ABS on sensor A continues
c: Air gap too large from bearing play or a sensor not seated fully
Sensor variant not matching the vehicle

C0653.d: C0653 means the circuit of left front sensor B sits below its valid level. Active wheel speed sensors usually signal through current steps; Allegro gives 7 and 14 mA as typical levels and a safe state below about 3.9 mA that a sensor uses to report its own fault.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Redundant braking or automated driving not available
c: Sensor B line chafed through and shorted to ground
Supply from the secondary control unit too low
Sensor in its fault (safe) state after an internal error

C0654.d: Here the circuit of the second left front sensor reads above its permitted level, typically a short to the battery feed or to the supply of another channel. That risk follows from the packaging: Continental's dual-element sensor gives each element its own two-wire cable but allows both to share one outer sheath, so a crushed or heat-damaged cable can affect both channels.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Possibly both speed signals of the wheel affected
c: Sensor B line shorted to battery voltage
Short between the two channels in a shared cable sheath
Internal fault in the second sensing channel

C0655.d: C0655 points to a second left front speed signal that drops out or jumps. Active sensors read the wheel through closely spaced sensing elements whose phase-shifted signals also give the rotation direction, as FenderBender explains, so small mechanical faults show up as irregular pulses.
s: Warning that comes and goes, often on rough roads or while steering
Automated or redundant brake functions intermittently withdrawn
c: Loose contact or partly broken wire that moves with the steering and suspension
Dirt or damage on the magnetic encoder
Excessive wheel bearing play changing the air gap

C0656.d: C0656 flags a mismatch between the B signal at the left front hub and the values it is checked against, typically sensor A on the same hub, while the circuit itself tests good. No carmaker publishes this code or its limits.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Automated or redundant brake functions withdrawn, ABS usually still active
c: Sensor not seated correctly, air gap out of tolerance
Damaged, dirty or partly demagnetized encoder ring
Sensor of a different type or side fitted

C0657.d: Here the module receives something on the second left front speed channel but decides that the fitted sensor is not the type it expects. No carmaker documents C0657, so the exact detection rule is unknown.
s: Warning appears soon after a sensor or hub replacement
Redundant braking or automated driving functions not available
c: Conventional single-channel sensor fitted instead of the dual-channel part
Sensor variant with other protocol or for the other side
Brake module not configured or coded for the fitted sensor

C0658.d: C0658 reports an open in the wiring of right front sensor B, so the module sees no supply current on that channel. Sensor B is the redundant partner found mainly in brake systems built for automated driving; ABS normally keeps running on sensor A, where an open would show as C0506.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Redundant braking or automated driving not available
c: Broken or torn sensor cable, often near the steering knuckle
Connector not latched, corroded or with spread terminals

C0659.d: The second right front speed signal arrives, but its quality or value does not fit. For sensors using the VDA AK protocol, Infineon's TLE5046SiC shows what a module can read besides speed: a 3-bit air gap gauge and, in one variant, a reserve bit that is set once the magnetic signal drops below twice the value at the limit air gap.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system, often only while driving
Automated functions withdrawn while ABS on sensor A continues
c: Air gap too large from wheel bearing play or a loose sensor holder
Encoder ring dirty, cracked or weakened

C065A.d: C065A means the current in the circuit of right front sensor B stays below its lowest valid level. TI's TPIC7218-Q1, an interface chip that powers and reads four wheel speed sensors, rates a current under about 4.5 mA as undercurrent and labels it a possible short to ground.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system right after switching on
Redundant braking or automated driving not available
c: Signal line chafed through and touching ground
Supply at the sensor too low, e.g. from contact resistance
Sensor reports an internal fault with its error current

C065B.d: In C065B the line of sensor B at the right front shows a level above its allowed window, which mostly means a short to the supply. TI's TPIC7218-Q1 sets this limit by sensor type: for active two-level sensors any current over 20 mA counts as overcurrent, for three-level VDA sensors only above 40 mA, in both cases marked as a possible short to battery.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system
Channel switched off by the module, redundant functions unavailable
c: Signal line shorted to battery voltage
Contact with the supply of another sensor channel in a shared cable
Sensor draws excessive current due to internal damage

C065C.d: C065C describes a second right front speed signal that vanishes now and then or carries irregular pulses. With AK protocol sensors, Pico's oscilloscope guide shows that the sensor keeps sending a data packet roughly every 147 ms even while the wheel stands still, so a break in that rhythm exposes a loose contact without the car moving.
s: Warning that comes and goes, e.g. on rough roads or while steering
Automated or redundant brake functions intermittently withdrawn
c: Loose contact in plug or cable, often where the cable flexes with steering
Encoder ring with dirt, metal chips or cracks
Interference from nearby high-current lines or damaged shielding

C065D.d: C065D says the second right front speed value disagrees with its comparison partners although no circuit fault is found. What it is compared with depends on the architecture.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system after a drive
Automated driving functions refused, ABS usually unaffected
c: Sensor B badly seated or air gap differing from sensor A
Encoder track damaged where only one element reads it
Disturbed data exchange between the brake control units

C065E.d: C065E means the module rejects the part fitted as the second speed sensor on the right front hub. Wheel speed sensors differ in their output scheme, and the receiving electronics are set up for one of them: TI's TPIC7218-Q1 is configured per sensor type, using two current thresholds for active sensors and four for VDA sensors that add 9 data bits.
s: Warning appears soon after a sensor or hub replacement
Redundant braking or automated driving functions not available
c: Replacement sensor with a different output protocol or variant
Single-channel sensor fitted where a dual-channel part belongs
Brake module not configured or coded for the fitted sensor

C065F.d: C065F reports that the second speed channel at the left rear wheel has no closed circuit. No carmaker publishes this code and no service bulletin mentions it, so the exact test is unknown.
s: Warning for brake or driver assistance system right after switching on
Functions relying on the second rear left signal not available
c: Broken lead or loose, corroded plug between sensor and module
Supply output for channel B in the brake module not switched on

C0660.d: C0660 means the wiring of sensor B at the left rear tests good, yet its output fails to act like a wheel speed: it may vanish at speed, jump or show an odd pulse pattern. No published service data defines the check.
s: Warning only appears while driving, often above a certain speed
Assistance functions withdrawn while ABS on sensor A continues
c: Sensor seated off-centre or too far from its encoder
Encoder ring worn, dirty or weakly magnetised

C0661.d: With C0661 the second left rear speed signal sits below the lowest level an intact sensor ever outputs, typically because the signal lead touches ground or the sensor feed has collapsed. No carmaker documents this code.
s: Warning for brake or stability system shortly after start
Emergency braking support of the electric parking brake may be restricted
c: Signal lead chafed through and touching ground
Sensor supply pulled down, e.g. by water in the plug

C0662.d: C0662 is stored when the second left rear speed channel reads above anything the sensor itself can deliver. NXP's KMI25 uses three current steps: about 7 mA at rest, 14 mA for a logic one of its data protocol and 28 mA for each speed pulse.
s: Warning lamp for ABS or stability control
Module switches channel B off, redundant functions unavailable
c: Signal lead shorted to battery voltage or to the sensor feed
Moisture or corrosion bridging pins in the connector
Sensor B drawing excessive current internally

C0663.d: Here the second left rear speed signal drops out for moments or jumps, without a lasting circuit fault. No public service data describes the code, so diagnosis has to follow the sensor principle.
s: Warning comes and goes, often on rough roads
Brief, unexpected stability or ABS interventions
c: Loose contact in plug or harness that opens on bumps
Encoder ring partly demagnetised or damaged
Interference from nearby motors or high-current cables

C0664.d: C0664 flags that the second left rear speed value disagrees with its reference speeds, although its circuit is sound. No carmaker publishes the comparison.
s: Warning set after a longer drive, not at start
Automated or redundant brake functions refused
c: Damaged or wrong encoder ring giving a false pulse count
Tyre of different size or heavily worn on the left rear
Sensor B losing pulses at high speed

C0665.d: C0665 says the part on the second left rear speed channel is not the one the module expects. No carmaker documents the code or how it identifies the part.
s: Warning appears right after a bearing, hub or sensor replacement
Redundant brake functions not available
c: Wheel bearing fitted with the encoder facing away from the sensor
Sensor made for a different encoder type or vehicle
Replacement hub without encoder ring fitted

C0666.d: The second speed channel at the right rear wheel is open: a wire, terminal or the sensor itself no longer conducts. C0666 is not documented by any carmaker.
s: Warning for brake or stability system on every start
Electric parking brake may only apply gradually while the switch is held
c: Harness or connector open at the right rear wheel
Sensor inside the hub bearing unit failed open
Input stage for channel B in the brake module defective

C0667.d: C0667 reports that the second right rear speed signal arrives but is not plausible, while the circuit itself is fine. No maker documents the code.
s: Warning mainly with load, towing or in fast bends
Stability control functions temporarily withdrawn
c: Worn or wrongly adjusted wheel bearing letting the gap vary
Axle shaft deflection under load or a bent shaft
Sensor not fully seated in its bore

C0668.d: C0668 points to a channel reading that is too low for the second right rear sensor. No carmaker documents the code, so the limit is not public.
s: Warning lamp for ABS or stability control
Redundant speed information at the right rear missing
c: Crushed or chafed lead leaking current to ground
High contact resistance lowering the sensor voltage
Sensor B internal current source defective

C0669.d: With C0669 the second right rear speed channel shows a level above the valid range, which usually means it is connected to a voltage source it should not see. No carmaker publishes this code.
s: Warning lamp right after switching on
Channel B switched off, assistance functions reduced
c: Signal lead shorted to battery voltage
Repaired or replacement harness wired to the wrong pins

C066A.d: C066A describes a second right rear speed signal that keeps dropping out or jumping. No carmaker documents it.
s: Warning appears and clears again during a drive
Speed of the right rear wheel jumps in live data
c: Encoder ring with metal swarf, cracks or weakened poles
Intermittent contact in plug or harness
Worn wheel bearing letting the encoder wobble

C066B.d: The second right rear speed value is electrically fine but disagrees with its references. No carmaker documents C066B or its limits.
s: Warning after a fast or long drive
Traction or stability functions temporarily reduced
c: Mismatched tyre size or tread depth at the right rear
Encoder with missing or extra pulses
Axle ratio or tyre data in the module not matching the vehicle

C066C.d: C066C indicates that the part on the second right rear speed channel differs from the one the module is set up for. No carmaker documents the code or its detection logic.
s: Warning appears right after work on the right rear hub
Redundant or automated brake functions not available
c: Hub or bearing from a variant without encoder or second sensor
Bearing fitted with the encoder side facing away from the sensor
Sensor of another type or vehicle fitted

C066D.d: C066D covers a fault in the transducer reporting the air pressure inside the service/spring brake chambers of an air-braked vehicle. No maker documents the code, but the diagnosis of real systems is published.
s: Parking brake indicator flashes, park status unknown
Automatic park functions such as rollaway protection unavailable
c: Sensor signal or 5 V supply shorted to ground or voltage
Pressure transducer in the valve module defective
Sensor outputs shorted together or connectors swapped

C066E.d: C066E means the measured chamber pressure is higher than the module allows in the present state. No maker documents the code, so its limit is not public.
s: Brake warning or fault message on the dash or trailer lamp
Harsh braking or overheated wheel ends after parking manoeuvres
c: Governor or pressure regulator letting system pressure rise too far
Anti-compound function not working, both forces add up

C066F.d: C066F reports chamber pressure below what the brake system needs. No maker documents this code.
s: Red brake or low-air warning, parking brake indicator flashing
Brakes dragging or spring brakes applying on their own
c: Leaking diaphragm, chamber seal or supply line
Insufficient reservoir pressure from compressor or dryer
Park valve or relay valve not delivering full pressure

C0670.d: C0670 is absent from the publicly available J2012 lists, but GM assigns it in its electronic damping control. In Saab's 2011 workshop data for the 9-5 and 9-4X it covers the vertical acceleration sensor at the left front wheel, which the suspension module supplies with 5 V and which answers with 0.5 to 4.5 V.
s: Service suspension message in the instrument cluster
Adaptive damping inactive, firmer or less controlled ride
c: Wheel acceleration sensor, its 5 V supply or signal wire faulty
Replacement sensor not compatible with early suspension module (GM PI0954)
Corroded or loose connector at the wheel housing

C0671.d: C0671 cannot be traced publicly: no publicly available J2012 list, no NHTSA bulletin, no GM keyword list and no Saab index contains it. GM even uses the neighbouring C0670 for a damping sensor and logs the electric park brake motor of the 2011 Saab 9-5 under C028A, with subcodes for shorts to plus or to ground, an open circuit and wrong frequency.
s: Park brake warning light or message
Right rear brake does not apply or does not release
c: Moisture or corrosion at the actuator plug in the wheel housing
Chafed or broken wire between module and actuator

C0680.d: Public evidence for C0680 is lacking: it is in none of the public J2012 tables, bulletins or maker indexes. The title describes a park brake controller that fails its own checks.
s: Park brake warning, function disabled or degraded
Brake cannot be applied, or only one more release is allowed
c: Calibration after brake service skipped or programming interrupted
Electronics inside the park brake or ABS/ESC module failed
Low battery voltage during self-test or programming
